- When sentiment is consistently bearish (negative or low) and model forecasts remain flat or upward, adjust downward by 2–5% to account for suppressed volatility.  
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >5% from prior day), model tends to overcorrect; reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 3–5 days to avoid overshoot.  
- If event count rises sharply (e.g., >15 events/30d) with net supply negative, model often underestimates downside risk; add 3–7% downward bias to forecast mean.  
- When sentiment swings from bullish to bearish within 3–5 days, model lags; shift forecast downward by 1–3% per day until sentiment stabilizes.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated 0.00 or negative values, model tends to ignore sentiment; force a 1–3% downward adjustment to forecast mean.  
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if recent 10–15 day mean is >60, model often overestimates; cap forecast at 60–65 unless sentiment is strongly bullish.  
- If supply net is negative and bullish sentiment is low, model tends to ignore supply constraints; add 2–5% downward bias to forecast.  
- When sentiment is mixed (e.g., 0.33–0.67) and model is flat, introduce 1–2% downward drift to reflect uncertainty.  
- If model forecast is >65 and true outcome is <60, apply 5–10% downward correction to avoid overconfidence in high-price regimes.  
- For 30d forecasts, if true outcome shows >3 consecutive days of decline, model often fails to recognize trend; apply 2–5% downward adjustment to next 5 days.
